cold_pressed.body:
A specification sheet for a potential new emollient ingredient we were reviewing listed the material as cold-pressed.

Cold-pressing is a temperature-controlled extraction process, typically kept below 49 degrees Celsius, designed to preserve the delicate fatty acid profiles of the plant material and prevent the degradation of heat-sensitive compounds. When an oil or emollient is exposed to higher temperatures during extraction, these beneficial components can oxidise or break down, changing how the ingredient behaves in the formulation. For a formulator, the distinction between a cold-pressed oil and one that has undergone standard heat processing is a matter of chemical integrity, not marketing nomenclature. It directly affects the performance and stability testing outcomes of the final product.

When I asked the supplier for the actual processing documentation, they eventually sent over a production log that showed temperatures between 70 and 85 degrees Celsius during extraction. That temperature range is indicative of standard heat processing, which is entirely different from cold-pressing. The cold-pressed claim on the specification sheet was either a labelling error or something else - I don't know which. What I do know is that we would have used the ingredient in our development work if I had trusted the specification sheet on its own and not asked for the primary logs.

I'm not making the claim that heat-processed ingredients are inherently bad or unsafe for use in skincare. Many excellent, stable formulations rely on heat-treated emollients. My point is simply that if a brand is paying for, formulating with, or claiming the benefits of a cold-pressed material, the physical reality of the manufacturing process must match the paperwork.

If you are formulating products or managing an ingredient supply chain, it is worth remembering that a specification sheet is a marketing document as much as a technical one. The only way to verify how an ingredient was actually treated is to ask for the production logs.

layering_order.body:
I received a message from a customer who was frustrated because the active serum she had been using for four months had suddenly stopped working, left her skin feeling congested, and felt as though it was no longer absorbing.

The serum itself hadn't changed, but her routine had. Two weeks prior, she had introduced a new, heavier occlusive moisturiser - likely a silicone-based formula given her description of the finish - and she was applying it before her serum. This is where basic formulation physics comes into play. An occlusive moisturiser is designed to sit on top of the skin barrier to seal in moisture and prevent water loss. When you apply a lightweight, water-based serum on top of a heavy, hydrophobic layer, the active ingredients simply cannot penetrate. They are physically blocked, leaving them to sit on top of the skin where they can cause surface congestion instead of doing their job.

I am not suggesting that heavy occlusive moisturisers are inherently bad or that they have no place in a routine. My point is simply that the physical structure of your products dictates how they must be layered if you want the active ingredients to actually reach their target.

When a skincare routine suddenly stops working, we tend to blame the product that we feel is failing us - in this case, the active serum. Because the serum is the product designed to target specific skin concerns, we assume its formulation has degraded or that our skin has suddenly rejected it. We don't often look at the passive steps in our routine as the culprit. But formulation chemistry doesn't work in isolation, and the absorption of any product is highly dependent on what sits beneath it.

Before concluding that a trusted product has stopped working or is suddenly congesting your skin, it is worth reviewing your layering order. Start with your thinnest, most water-heavy formulations and finish with your heaviest occlusives. Sometimes the solution doesn't require replacing a product, but simply rearranging the order in which it meets your skin.

batch_14.body:
Our stability testing for batch fourteen returned pH data that did not match our established baseline. When we investigated the discrepancy with our supplier, we discovered they had altered the preservative blend without a direct notification, sending a revised specification sheet three months ago that had been overlooked. The new preservative system is more acidic than the original version, causing the finished product's pH to drop by about 0.4 units. In our formulation, this shift was enough to push the batch outside the optimal pH range required for our emollient blend to remain stable and perform correctly.

The batch itself isn't unsafe, but the altered acidity has modified the final texture in a way that our customers would notice, which is why we're holding it. This incident highlights an industry reality that is rarely discussed: a raw material reorder is never automatically identical to the previous one. Suppliers make adjustments to their manufacturing processes, source materials, or preservative packages for their own stability or supply chain reasons, and these changes often occur without explicit warnings to the brands buying them. If a brand isn't actively auditing the Certificate of Analysis - the CoA - for every single incoming batch against their original baseline documentation, these silent formula changes won't be caught until the finished product is already on retail shelves.

I want to be precise about the point I'm making. I'm not suggesting that raw material suppliers are behaving maliciously, nor am I saying that minor formulation shifts are inherently dangerous. I'm arguing that the responsibility for verifying formulation consistency rests entirely with the brand, rather than the supplier or the contract manufacturer.

For those formulating or managing production, the only reliable safeguard is to establish a strict protocol where no raw material is cleared for compounding until its CoA has been manually checked against the initial standardised baseline. For consumers, it's worth remembering that consistency in skincare isn't a given - it's the result of constant, tedious documentation checks behind the scenes.
